title: Resolve the same conflict once, not five times
summary: A long-lived branch hits the same conflict on every rebase. Turn on rerere and git replays your resolution automatically, for as long as the conflict keeps coming back.
mental_model: rerere — reuse recorded resolution — fingerprints each conflict by its two sides. When it sees the same fingerprint again, it applies the resolution you gave last time. It resolves the file but deliberately does not stage it, so you still get to look.

commit.message: Raise pool size for the new workload

steps.title: Turn on rerere before you need it
steps.why: It records nothing retroactively, so switching it on after a painful conflict is too late. This is a config line worth having globally on every machine you use.

steps.title: Hit the conflict and resolve it by hand — once
steps.why: Standard conflict, standard resolution. The difference is the line git prints: 'Recorded preimage for settings.py'. It has fingerprinted the conflict before you touched it.
steps.expect: A conflict, plus a message about recording the preimage.

steps.title: Write the resolution
steps.why: 50 is what the new workload needs. Committing the merge makes rerere store the resolution against that fingerprint — 'Recorded resolution for settings.py'.
steps.expect: An entry in .git/rr-cache — the memory that makes the next step work.

steps.title: Undo the merge, as if you had rebased instead
steps.why: This simulates the real situation: the merge gets thrown away and the same two sides collide again. On a long-lived branch this happens on every single rebase onto a moving main.
steps.expect: Back to main's version, merge gone.

steps.title: Hit the identical conflict again
steps.why: This time git says 'Resolved settings.py using previous resolution'. The file already contains 50 — no markers, no thinking, no chance of resolving it differently by accident.
steps.expect: The file is resolved automatically, but still listed as unmerged.

verify.label: rerere replayed the resolution automatically
verify.hint: the resolution had to be recorded once, with rerere already enabled

steps.title: Notice what rerere deliberately did not do
steps.why: It resolved the file but left it unstaged. That is intentional: rerere is confident about the mechanics, not about whether the resolution is still correct. You review, then stage.

steps.title: Forget a resolution you regret
steps.why: If you resolved something wrongly, rerere will keep replaying that mistake. `git rerere forget <path>` drops the recorded answer so the next conflict asks you again.
steps.expect: Nothing pending — the cache is tidy.

verify.label: rerere is enabled in this repository
the recorded resolution was applied on the second conflict

pitfalls: rerere replays your previous answer even when the surrounding code has changed underneath it. Review what it staged — it resolves, it does not think.
It is per-clone and lives in `.git/rr-cache`, so a fresh clone starts with no memory. There is no way to share resolutions between people.
Enable it before the painful week, not during. Nothing is recorded retroactively.
`git rerere forget <path>` is the fix for a resolution you got wrong; without it the mistake repeats forever.
